<div id="page-header"><div class="header-basic style-dark">

																	<h1 class="header-title h1"><span>Mobile Robots in Retail: Inventory Automation</span></h1><div class="post-info"><div class="date-info">2 November 2026</div><div class="category-info"><span>|</span>In <a href="https://robotnik.eu/category/robotic-applications/" title="View all posts in Robotic applications">Robotic applications</a></div><div class="author-info"><span>|</span>By <a href="https://robotnik.eu/author/alerma/">Andrea Lerma Casany</a></div></div>
																</div>
															</div>
														</div></div>
												</div></div><script type="text/javascript">UNCODE.initHeader();</script><article id="post-60694" class="page-body style-light-bg post-60694 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-robotic-applications tag-automate-repetitive-tasks tag-autonomous-mobile-robots tag-custom-robotic-solutions tag-manipulador-movil-en tag-mobile-manipulator tag-robotnik-robots tag-robots-moviles-autonomos-en">
          <div class="post-wrapper">
          	<div class="post-body"><div class="row-container">
        							<div class="row row-parent un-sidebar-layout col-std-gutter no-top-padding no-bottom-padding limit-width">
												<div class="row-inner">
													<div class="col-lg-8">
											<div class="post-content style-light"><div data-parent="true" class="vc_row row-container" id="row-unique-0"><div class="row limit-width row-parent"><div class="wpb_row row-inner"><div class="wpb_column pos-top pos-center align_left column_parent col-lg-12 single-internal-gutter"><div class="uncol style-light"  ><div class="uncoltable"><div class="uncell no-block-padding" ><div class="uncont" ><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Retail inventory management requires knowing which products are available, in what quantities and where they are located. Sales, returns and movements between the stockroom and sales floor continually change this information, making it difficult for records to reflect the store’s actual inventory.</span></p>
<p><a href="https://robotnik.eu/products/mobile-robots/"><b>Mobile robots</b></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> can automate data collection routes using RFID readers, cameras and specialized software. The information collected helps teams check stock, identify discrepancies and organize replenishment.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">At Robotnik, we develop </span><b>modular platforms for integrators and technology companies to build inventory applications</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. Robin, developed by Keonn on our RB-THERON platform, demonstrates how autonomous movement can be combined with RFID reading and dedicated inventory software.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h2 class="h2 text-accent-color" ><span>Why Mobile Robots Are Entering Retail Operations</span></h2></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Manual inventory checks involve walking through the store, identifying SKUs and comparing quantities. In stores with extensive product ranges, repeating these checks takes up a significant portion of employees’ time.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Mobile robotics allows scheduled routes across the sales floor and stock areas to collect information regularly. Staff can then focus their checks on products or locations where discrepancies have been detected.</span></p>
<p><b>Sharing inventory data between the sales floor, stockroom and warehouse helps teams track product availability and movements.</b><span style="font-weight: 400;"> Sharing information about quantities and movements helps teams understand whether products are available for sale, held in the stockroom or require further checks. This complements</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/automated-inventory-management-by-autonomous-warehouse-robots/"> <span style="font-weight: 400;">automated warehouse inventory management</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">, while addressing the specific needs of the store.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h2 class="h2 text-accent-color" ><span>How Mobile Robots Turn Shelf Data into Inventory Decisions</span></h2></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h3 class="h3" ><span>Autonomous Inventory Scanning</span></h3></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">An inventory application combines platform navigation with the devices needed to identify products. The robot travels through defined areas while the system records readings and associates them with the retailer’s SKUs.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Routes can follow </span><b>daily, overnight or other scheduled inventory routines</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. Planning must account for store activity, accessible areas and staff tasks to minimize disruption.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Automation makes the process repeatable without requiring a full manual count on every round. Detected discrepancies still require an operational response, such as checking a location, correcting a record or finding a product.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h3>Shelf Analysis and Stockout Detection</h3>
</div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">The required technology depends on what needs to be checked. </span><b>RFID product identification and visual shelf analysis are different applications.</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">An RFID system reads tags associated with products. A computer vision application can analyze shelf images to detect gaps, misplaced products or deviations from the planogram, which defines the intended product layout.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Price verification requires recognizing visible information and comparing it with pricing records. These functions need cameras, software and development tailored to the environment and products.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Adding a mobile base therefore </span><b>does not automatically provide empty-shelf detection, price checking or misplaced-product identification</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. These capabilities depend on the modules integrated into the final application.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h3>Smart Replenishment and Product Availability</h3>
</div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Readings allow recorded inventory to be compared with detected products. If an SKU is listed as available but is not detected in its expected location, staff can investigate whether it remains in the stockroom, has been moved or reflects a recording discrepancy.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">A product may be available in the stockroom while missing from the sales floor. Linking readings to recorded locations helps teams distinguish </span><b>a replenishment need from a lack of inventory</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Integration with inventory and replenishment systems allows alerts and task lists to be generated. Teams can prioritize shelves according to product availability and store criteria.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">The robot supplies data that helps trigger these tasks. </span><b>Physical replenishment is a separate operation</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">, performed by staff or by a manipulation application developed for that purpose.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h2 class="h2 text-accent-color" ><span>Technologies That Make Retail Mobile Robots Useful</span></h2></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Technology selection starts with the products to be identified and the information the retailer needs:</span></p>
<ul>
<li style="font-weight: 400;" aria-level="1"><b>RFID and barcode scanning:</b><span style="font-weight: 400;"> RFID identifies tagged products using radio waves without requiring each tag to be scanned visually. Barcode readers require visible, legible codes. Reading coverage depends on the devices, product labeling and operating conditions.</span></li>
<li style="font-weight: 400;" aria-level="1"><b>Computer vision:</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">  Cameras and image-processing software, including AI models where appropriate, can identify shelf gaps, misplaced products and planogram deviations. Each function must be developed and validated for the application.</span></li>
<li style="font-weight: 400;" aria-level="1"><b>LiDAR and SLAM:</b><span style="font-weight: 400;"> Support robot localization and navigation through mapped spaces.</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/autonomous-navigation-and-mobile-robots/"> <span style="font-weight: 400;">Autonomous navigation</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> allows the platform to respond to detected obstacles, subject to available space and configured limits.</span></li>
<li style="font-weight: 400;" aria-level="1"><b>System integration:</b><span style="font-weight: 400;"> Connections with WMS, ERP, inventory platforms or replenishment tools transfer results to the systems used by store teams.</span></li>
</ul>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">On compatible platforms,</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/ros-2-robot-operating-system-overview-and-key-points-for-robotics-software/"> <b>ROS 2</b></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> supports communication between components and the development of application-specific functions.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Collaborative platforms can share spaces with people using their detection and protection systems. Deployment must consider routes, robot dimensions and the</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/safety-requirements-for-industrial-robots-guarantee-of-collaboration-and-efficiency/"> <span style="font-weight: 400;">safety of the complete application</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">.</span></p>
</div><div class="uncode-single-media  text-left"><div class="single-wrapper" style="max-width: 100%;"><div class="tmb tmb-light  tmb-media-first tmb-media-last tmb-content-overlay tmb-no-bg"><div class="t-inside"><div class="t-entry-visual"><div class="t-entry-visual-tc"><div class="uncode-single-media-wrapper"><img decoding="async" class="wp-image-60714" src="data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201130%20850'%3E%3C/svg%3E" width="1130" height="850" alt="" data-lazy-srcset="https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA.png 1130w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-300x226.png 300w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-1024x770.png 1024w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-768x578.png 768w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-350x263.png 350w" data-lazy-sizes="(max-width: 1130px) 100vw, 1130px" data-lazy-src="https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA.png" /><noscript><img decoding="async" class="wp-image-60714" src="https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA.png" width="1130" height="850" alt="" srcset="https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA.png 1130w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-300x226.png 300w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-1024x770.png 1024w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-768x578.png 768w, https://robotnik.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RB-THERON-PORTADA-350x263.png 350w" sizes="(max-width: 1130px) 100vw, 1130px" /></noscript></div>

				</div></div></div></div></div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h2 class="h2 text-accent-color" ><span>Benefits of Using Mobile Robots in Retail</span></h2></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h3 class="h3" ><span>More Accurate Inventory Data</span></h3></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Scheduled rounds allow data to be collected </span><b>more frequently and through a consistent procedure</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. This makes it easier to detect discrepancies and check whether an issue persists between rounds.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Accuracy depends on reading coverage and the correct association of identifiers, SKUs and locations. Teams also need to know when data was collected and which areas were checked to interpret the results.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">This information helps retailers target checks and reduce differences between recorded inventory and detected stock.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h3 class="h3" ><span>Improved Operational Efficiency and Customer Experience</span></h3></div><div class="clear"></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Automating part of the counting process </span><b>reduces repetitive manual tasks</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">, allowing staff to spend more time on customer service, replenishment and resolving issues.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Checks can focus on locations flagged by the system, rather than inspecting every shelf equally often. More reliable inventory information also helps staff locate products and answer availability questions.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">When teams act on the findings, better stock visibility supports replenishment and helps keep products available to shoppers.</span></p>
</div><div class="vc_custom_heading_wrap "><div class="heading-text el-text" ><h2 class="h2 text-accent-color" ><span>Robotnik Mobile Robots for Smarter Inventory Automation</span></h2></div><div 				</div></div></div></div></div><div class="uncode_text_column" ><p><a href="https://robotnik.eu/products/mobile-robots/rb-theron/"><b>RB-THERON</b></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> is a modular indoor platform that can integrate readers, cameras and other devices for retail applications. </span><b>Robotnik provides the mobile base, control and navigation capabilities</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">, while specialized third-party technology completes the inventory application.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Robin, developed by Keonn on RB-THERON, shows how these functions come together. Robotnik’s platform provides autonomous movement, while </span><b>Keonn integrates RFID reading technology and dedicated inventory software</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. This is an example of</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/custom-robots-in-industry-and-manufacturing/"> <span style="font-weight: 400;">application development on a modular Robotnik platform</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">During a route, the RFID system identifies tagged products and collects readings for the inventory application to process. Autonomous movement removes the need for an employee to walk through the space with a handheld reader on every round.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">The platform’s modular design allows readers, cameras and other devices to be configured for the application. The open architecture connects the specialized application with</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/software-solutions/"> <span style="font-weight: 400;">Robotnik’s control and navigation software</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">.</span></p>
<p><b>Robin’s application is RFID inventory scanning.</b><span style="font-weight: 400;"> Visual shelf analysis and price verification require separate modules.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">For projects involving manipulation,</span><a href="https://robotnik.eu/products/mobile-manipulators/rb-kairos/"> <b>RB-KAIROS+</b></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> supports the development of pick-and-place operations. Retail applications require the products, gripping method and working locations to be defined; it is not a standard shelf-replenishment solution.</span></p>

The final capabilities depend on the reading devices, software and integrations developed for each application.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Robin illustrates this approach: </span><b>Robotnik provides mobility, while Keonn integrates RFID reading and inventory software</b><span style="font-weight: 400;">. Together, these technologies support inventory automation in retail.</span></p>

Retail inventory management requires knowing which products are available, in what quantities and where they are located. Sales, returns and movements between the stockroom and sales floor continually change this information, making it difficult for records to reflect the store’s actual inventory. Mobile robots can automate data collection routes using RFID readers, cameras and specialized software. The information collected helps teams check stock, identify discrepancies and organize replenishment. At Robotnik, we develop modular platforms for integrators and technology companies to build inventory applications. Robin, developed by Keonn on our RB-THERON platform, demonstrates how autonomous movement can be combined with RFID reading and dedicated inventory software.

Why Mobile Robots Are Entering Retail Operations

Manual inventory checks involve walking through the store, identifying SKUs and comparing quantities. In stores with extensive product ranges, repeating these checks takes up a significant portion of employees’ time. Mobile robotics allows scheduled routes across the sales floor and stock areas to collect information regularly. Staff can then focus their checks on products or locations where discrepancies have been detected. Sharing inventory data between the sales floor, stockroom and warehouse helps teams track product availability and movements. Sharing information about quantities and movements helps teams understand whether products are available for sale, held in the stockroom or require further checks. This complements automated warehouse inventory management, while addressing the specific needs of the store.

How Mobile Robots Turn Shelf Data into Inventory Decisions

Autonomous Inventory Scanning

An inventory application combines platform navigation with the devices needed to identify products. The robot travels through defined areas while the system records readings and associates them with the retailer’s SKUs. Routes can follow daily, overnight or other scheduled inventory routines. Planning must account for store activity, accessible areas and staff tasks to minimize disruption. Automation makes the process repeatable without requiring a full manual count on every round. Detected discrepancies still require an operational response, such as checking a location, correcting a record or finding a product.

Shelf Analysis and Stockout Detection

The required technology depends on what needs to be checked. RFID product identification and visual shelf analysis are different applications. An RFID system reads tags associated with products. A computer vision application can analyze shelf images to detect gaps, misplaced products or deviations from the planogram, which defines the intended product layout. Price verification requires recognizing visible information and comparing it with pricing records. These functions need cameras, software and development tailored to the environment and products. Adding a mobile base therefore does not automatically provide empty-shelf detection, price checking or misplaced-product identification. These capabilities depend on the modules integrated into the final application.

Smart Replenishment and Product Availability

Readings allow recorded inventory to be compared with detected products. If an SKU is listed as available but is not detected in its expected location, staff can investigate whether it remains in the stockroom, has been moved or reflects a recording discrepancy. A product may be available in the stockroom while missing from the sales floor. Linking readings to recorded locations helps teams distinguish a replenishment need from a lack of inventory. Integration with inventory and replenishment systems allows alerts and task lists to be generated. Teams can prioritize shelves according to product availability and store criteria. The robot supplies data that helps trigger these tasks. Physical replenishment is a separate operation, performed by staff or by a manipulation application developed for that purpose.

Technologies That Make Retail Mobile Robots Useful

Technology selection starts with the products to be identified and the information the retailer needs: RFID and barcode scanning: RFID identifies tagged products using radio waves without requiring each tag to be scanned visually. Barcode readers require visible, legible codes. Reading coverage depends on the devices, product labeling and operating conditions.

Computer vision: Cameras and image-processing software, including AI models where appropriate, can identify shelf gaps, misplaced products and planogram deviations. Each function must be developed and validated for the application.

LiDAR and SLAM: Support robot localization and navigation through mapped spaces. Autonomous navigation allows the platform to respond to detected obstacles, subject to available space and configured limits.

System integration: Connections with WMS, ERP, inventory platforms or replenishment tools transfer results to the systems used by store teams. On compatible platforms, ROS 2 supports communication between components and the development of application-specific functions. Collaborative platforms can share spaces with people using their detection and protection systems. Deployment must consider routes, robot dimensions and the safety of the complete application.

Benefits of Using Mobile Robots in Retail

More Accurate Inventory Data

Scheduled rounds allow data to be collected more frequently and through a consistent procedure. This makes it easier to detect discrepancies and check whether an issue persists between rounds. Accuracy depends on reading coverage and the correct association of identifiers, SKUs and locations. Teams also need to know when data was collected and which areas were checked to interpret the results. This information helps retailers target checks and reduce differences between recorded inventory and detected stock.

Improved Operational Efficiency and Customer Experience

Automating part of the counting process reduces repetitive manual tasks, allowing staff to spend more time on customer service, replenishment and resolving issues. Checks can focus on locations flagged by the system, rather than inspecting every shelf equally often. More reliable inventory information also helps staff locate products and answer availability questions. When teams act on the findings, better stock visibility supports replenishment and helps keep products available to shoppers.

Robotnik Mobile Robots for Smarter Inventory Automation

RB-THERON is a modular indoor platform that can integrate readers, cameras and other devices for retail applications. Robotnik provides the mobile base, control and navigation capabilities, while specialized third-party technology completes the inventory application. Robin, developed by Keonn on RB-THERON, shows how these functions come together. Robotnik’s platform provides autonomous movement, while Keonn integrates RFID reading technology and dedicated inventory software. This is an example of application development on a modular Robotnik platform. During a route, the RFID system identifies tagged products and collects readings for the inventory application to process. Autonomous movement removes the need for an employee to walk through the space with a handheld reader on every round. The platform’s modular design allows readers, cameras and other devices to be configured for the application. The open architecture connects the specialized application with Robotnik’s control and navigation software. Robin’s application is RFID inventory scanning. Visual shelf analysis and price verification require separate modules. For projects involving manipulation, RB-KAIROS+ supports the development of pick-and-place operations. Retail applications require the products, gripping method and working locations to be defined; it is not a standard shelf-replenishment solution.

Conclusion: Mobile Robots as a Key Driver of Retail Efficiency
